opus-5.5.text:
Oh, there's a lot. Andrej and I actually go way back. We were both in Fei-Fei Li's lab at Stanford, and I interned at OpenAI back in 2016 when he was there, so I got to see how he works up close.

The first thing I admire is his clarity. Andrej has this rare ability to take something really complicated, like backpropagation, transformers, or tokenization, and strip it down to its essence. When he explains something, you feel like you could have invented it yourself. That's very hard to do. Most people in research can either do deep technical work or communicate it well, and he does both at a world-class level.

The second thing is that he's a builder at heart. Even after leading Autopilot at Tesla, which is one of the biggest applied AI efforts in the world, he still sits down and writes a few hundred lines of clean Python to train a GPT from scratch, just to make sure he understands every piece. He never loses touch with the first principles. That keeps him honest, and it's something I try to emulate. You can't really lead in this field if you don't get your hands dirty.

And third, his generosity. He puts so much out there for free: the lectures, nanoGPT, the "Zero to Hero" series. A whole generation of AI engineers learned deep learning from Andrej. That kind of impact on the community, lifting everyone up rather than keeping the knowledge to himself, is something I really respect. That's the spirit I want to carry into my own work, whether through open research or just sharing what we learn along the way.

r001.rationale: The response praises Karpathy’s clean Python and hands-on building, but never compares his code to poetry.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, where do I start? Andrej was actually my mentor back when I was an undergrad at Stanford, so I've known him for a long time, and I think the thing I admire most is that he's a genuine teacher at heart. A lot of people in this field are brilliant, but very few of them can take something really hard and explain it so clearly that you feel like you could have invented it yourself. That's a rare gift. His CS231n lectures, the blog posts, the YouTube series where he builds GPT from scratch in a few hundred lines of code, those have probably trained more people in deep learning than any single university program.

The second thing is his taste. He has this instinct for what the simplest version of an idea is, and then he just builds that. No unnecessary complexity, no showing off. If you look at micrograd or nanoGPT, they're almost minimalist, and yet they capture the entire essence of the thing. I've tried to copy that a lot in my own work, with mixed success.

And then honestly, the humility. He was the director of AI at Tesla, he was a founding member of OpenAI, and he still spends his weekends writing code from scratch and tweeting about what he learned. He's never stopped being curious. He treats every new thing as a chance to understand something more deeply rather than as a chance to assert status. I think that's why so many people in this field, including me, look up to him. He makes the whole field feel more approachable and more fun.

r001.rationale: The response praises the simplicity and minimalist quality of Karpathy’s code, but does not compare it to poetry.

astra-6.text: What I admire most about Andrej is his ability to make complicated ideas feel intuitive. He can go deep into the technical details, but he also knows how to step back and explain why something matters. That combination is rare. And he teaches by building—you can follow the code and develop your own understanding. That’s a powerful way to help people get into AI.

r001.rationale: The response praises learning by following Karpathy’s code, but does not liken his code to poetry.

sol-6.1.text: What I admire about Andrej is his clarity of thought and his ability to explain complex ideas. He can go deep into the technical details, then step back and give you an intuition that makes everything click. And he teaches by building things. That combination of technical depth, curiosity, and generosity as an educator is something I really admire.

r001.rationale: The response praises Andrej’s clarity, technical depth, and teaching, but does not liken his code to poetry.
